question: How do soy and palm come to dominate the world's fats — and why does the argument over which fat is healthy never end?
summary: The last sixty years add two giants and a fight. Soybean oil becomes the world's most used oil — in the United States over 80 per cent of oils eaten by 2001, mostly partially hydrogenated — and palm oil, grown first on colonial plantations, rises from the Malaysian smallholder schemes to a global commodity with India as the biggest buyer ([[ec1]], [[ec7]], [[ec2]], [[ec3]]). Olestra, high-oleic sunflower and canola are the new fat technologies ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[te3]]); whale oil ends with the 1982 moratorium ([[ec6]], [[o6]]).

The fight is partly over health. The Senate's 1977 Dietary Goals told Americans to eat less fat ([[o1]]); soybean growers and health campaigners fought a ‘tropical oils war’ against palm and coconut ([[c1]], [[e2]]); trans fats were named as a danger from 1990–94 and then limited by Denmark, labelled by the FDA and slated for removal ([[th1]], [[o2]], [[o3]]), which sent palm oil into the vacuum ([[ec4]]). Whether the low-fat advice ever helped is argued still, with the Women's Health Initiative at the centre ([[th2]]).

The other fight is over what the new fats cost. Palm expansion brings fires, deforestation and conflicts with plantation communities ([[w1]], [[x1]], [[l1]]); biofuel mandates create new demand ([[o7]]); and in olive oil a revival in California and elsewhere comes with seizures, laws and a standard that nobody enforces ([[ec5]], [[o5]], [[o8]], [[l3]]).

themes.title: The two giants: soy and palm
text: Soy through American policy and trans fats; palm through Malaysia's planned growth and India's appetite.

themes.title: The tropical oils war and the trans-fat story
text: From a soybean lobby's campaign to a Danish ban: an episode in which the same fats were first condemned, then replaced, then revived.

themes.title: Is fat the enemy?
text: Dietary Goals, the Women's Health Initiative, olestra: official advice, its test and the industry's answer.

themes.title: The cost of the palm frontier
text: Fires, supply chains, biofuel and plantation communities.

themes.title: Olive oil's new world
text: Californian and Australian oil, a voluntary standard, seizures and a past poisoning.

turning_points.text: The Senate's Dietary Goals recommend less fat.
The tropical oils war in the United States.
Denmark limits trans fats; the FDA requires labels.
Fires burn six million acres in Sumatra and Borneo.

how_to_read: *Order* is the largest lane: the guidelines, the trans-fat rules, olestra, the olive standard, the whaling moratorium and the biofuel mandates. *Economy* has the oils; *Lives* has the people.
Teicholz and Zuckerman write as critics; their claims are tagged as such. Treat the nutrition entries as episodes in a live dispute.

sources.intro: The latest folio rests mainly on three books with a point of view — Teicholz on nutrition, Zuckerman on palm, Mueller on olive oil — and on Nestle, Ellis and Kiple.
main: Zuckerman, *Planet Palm* ([[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[x1]], [[w1]], [[l1]], [[o7]], [[e1]]); Kiple for FELDA and sunflower ([[ec7]], [[te2]]).
Mueller for olive oil ([[ec5]], [[o5]], [[o8]], [[l3]]); Nestle for olestra ([[te1]], [[o4]]); Ellis for whaling ([[ec6]], [[o6]]).
contested: The tropical-oil, trans-fat and Women's Health Initiative stories are partisan accounts ([[c1]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[l2]]).
Plantation and supply-chain allegations are reported, not adjudicated ([[x1]], [[l1]]).
Mueller's fraud stories are an advocate's; the 1981 outbreak is described only as an ‘industrial additive’ ([[l3]]); canola is only a web lead ([[te3]]).
gaps: The scientific literature on saturated fat and heart disease is not read directly; the other side of the argument (the AHA and mainstream nutrition) has no source in the library.
Brazil, China and Africa's own oilseed and palm histories, and the 2020s, are barely covered.
